readerTitle: Why hostage negotiators slow down when everything says hurry
caseNote: 실제 기관 사례 (NYPD 인질협상팀, 1972년 뮌헨, 1993년 웨이코) + 실제 연구 (FBI 행동 변화 계단 모델) + 가상 적용 (사내 예산 갈등, 식품 유통사)
insight: 감정이 끓는 협상에서는 설득할 권리를 먼저 얻어야 한다. 듣기와 관계가 쌓이기 전에 내놓은 제안은 아무리 좋아도 거절된다.
misconception: 상대가 화가 났을 때는 빨리 좋은 해결책이나 양보를 내놓을수록 협상이 잘 풀린다.

sources.text: 1972 뮌헨 올림픽 인질 사건 (이스라엘 선수단 11명 사망, 공항 구출 작전 실패): 주요 언론 및 역사 기록 (예: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Munich Massacre')
NYPD Hostage Negotiation Team 창설(1973), Harvey Schlossberg·Frank Bolz의 역할: NYPD 및 다수 언론 기록 (예: Schlossberg 부고 기사, The New York Times, 2023)
Vecchi, G. M., Van Hasselt, V. B., & Romano, S. J. (2005). Crisis (hostage) negotiation: current strategies and issues in high-risk conflict resolution. Aggression and Violent Behavior, 10(5).
U.S. Department of Justice (1993). Report to the Deputy Attorney General on the Events at Waco, Texas, 및 관련 외부 전문가 검토 보고서

factChecks.note: 뮌헨 사건: 이스라엘 선수단 11명 사망, 서독 당국의 공항 구출 시도 실패. 카드에는 숫자 없이 'all the hostages were killed'로만 적었습니다. 사망자 총수(경찰관 1명 포함 여부)는 쓰지 않았습니다.
NYPD 인질협상팀이 1973년에 만들어졌고 심리학자이자 경찰관인 Harvey Schlossberg와 형사 Frank Bolz가 주도했다는 점을 확인하세요. 'contain and negotiate', 'time is on our side' 원칙은 이들의 접근법을 설명할 때 흔히 쓰이는 표현이며, 정확한 인용으로 쓰지 않았습니다.
2번 카드의 결정 상황은 1973년 당시 경찰 지휘관이 겪던 전형적 상황을 재구성한 것입니다. 특정 사건(예: 1973년 1월 브루클린 스포츠용품점 인질 사건)의 세부를 지어내지 않도록 일반화했습니다.
행동 변화 계단 모델의 단계명(active listening, empathy, rapport, influence, behavioral change)은 Vecchi 외(2005) 원문으로 확인하세요.
웨이코(1993): 51일간 대치, 협상팀과 전술팀의 압박(전기 차단, 소음 등)이 엇갈렸다는 지적은 법무부 보고서와 외부 전문가 검토에 나옵니다. 카드에는 사망자 수 없이 'ended in a fire that killed dozens of people'로 적었으니 표현을 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why hostage negotiators slow down when everything says hurry
body: In 1972, at the Munich Olympics, a rushed police rescue went wrong and all the Israeli hostages were killed.
Within a year, the New York Police Department built something new: a team whose main tools were a phone, patience and **time**.

image.label: A police negotiator on a phone, a clock behind him
image.brief: 1970년대 분위기의 차분한 일러스트. 경찰 협상가가 낡은 전화기를 들고 귀 기울이는 모습, 뒤편 벽시계 바늘이 천천히 움직이는 느낌. 실제 경찰 휘장이나 로고는 쓰지 않음. 폭력적인 장면 없이.

cards.title: Armed robbers are trapped inside with hostages.
body: It's 1973. You command the police outside a store. The robbers are panicking and shouting threats. Your officers have the building surrounded, and the press wants an ending.

options.text: Move in fast, before they settle in
options.feedback: Speed ends it quickly if it works. But you hit them at peak panic, which is exactly when people do the worst things.

options.text: Give them a firm deadline to surrender
options.feedback: A deadline shows strength, but it also adds pressure to people who are already overloaded, and it locks you in if they miss it.

options.text: Keep them contained, open a line, and mostly listen
options.feedback: You give up a quick ending. In return, panic has time to fade and someone they trust has time to form. This became NYPD's approach.

cards.title: New York made time its ally.
body: In 1973 the NYPD formed one of the first dedicated hostage negotiation teams, led by Harvey Schlossberg, a detective trained in psychology, and detective Frank Bolz.

Their idea, often summed up as *contain and negotiate*, was simple. Strong emotions peak early and then fade. Every hour of talking lowers the heat and builds a relationship. So unless lives are in immediate danger, slow down.
Police forces around the world, and later the FBI, adopted the approach.

cards.title: Earn the right to persuade.
body: FBI researchers later described the process as a **stairway**: listen, show you understand, build rapport, and only then try to influence. Changed behavior comes last.

The order is the point. A sensible proposal made on the first step usually fails, because the other side isn't ready to hear anything from you yet. Negotiators climb the steps in sequence, and they accept that it takes time.

image.label: Five-step stairway from listening to changed behavior
image.brief: 계단 다섯 칸 인포그래픽. 아래부터 "Listen", "Understand", "Rapport", "Influence", "Change". 맨 아래에서 맨 위로 바로 점프하려는 화살표에 X 표시.

cards.title: The angry team lead down the hall.
body: A finance director must cut a product team's budget by a fifth. The team lead hears about it secondhand and is furious.

Version one: she walks in with a well-built spreadsheet of options. He rejects every one. Version two: the first meeting has no spreadsheet. She asks what the cut would break, repeats his worries back, and agrees to meet again. A week later, he brings his own options.
cards.softwareNote: After a major outage, an enterprise customer threatening to cancel rarely wants a credit in the first call. Account teams that listen first, then come back with a plan, usually keep more accounts than teams that open with a discount.

cards.title: Slowing down only works if you mean it.
body: At Waco, Texas, in 1993, a 51-day standoff ended in a fire that killed dozens of people. Later reviews found that negotiators were building trust while tactical teams added pressure, such as cutting power. Each move undid the other.
Two lessons for business. Mixed signals reset the stairway, so don't listen warmly while a colleague sends threats. And time is an ally only when waiting doesn't make your position worse.

cards.title: Your biggest grocery customer is furious.
body: You run sales at a regional food distributor. A shortage left your largest grocery chain with empty shelves before a holiday weekend. Their buyer calls, angry, and says they're talking to other distributors.

options.text: Offer a discount on the next three orders right away
options.feedback: It looks generous, but you skip the steps that make it land. You also teach the buyer that anger earns concessions.

options.text: Explain the cause and the new safeguards in detail
options.feedback: The facts matter, but explaining now sounds like defending. It's the right content on the wrong step.

options.text: Ask what it cost them, repeat it back, and promise a written plan tomorrow
options.feedback: You give up a fast fix. In return, the buyer feels heard and is ready to listen when your plan arrives.

cards.title: Listen first. Persuade later.
body: When emotions run high, a good offer made too early gets rejected. Climb the steps in order, and let time work for you.
**Try it today:** in your next tense conversation, don't propose anything in the first ten minutes. Just ask, listen and summarize.
